activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Victoria spread three bean plants across the library table, each in its own foam cup, and waited for Marek and Lou to stop arguing about whose turn it was with the good chair. The plants were for the science fair, and the fair was in nine days, which felt both far away and inevitable, like a bus you can hear but not see yet.

"Okay, here's the setup," she said. "Cup one gets fertilizer every Monday. Cup two gets double fertilizer. Cup three gets plain water only." She turned cup three so its label faced them. "This one is my control group. It gets no change at all, so I have something to compare the other two against."

Lou leaned over the cups, chewing the end of a pencil. "That's the sad one. It's tiny." He poked the soil with one finger, and something small and pale curled in the disturbed dirt. Marek shouted something about a larva, which made a woman at the next table shush them so hard her glasses slid down her nose. "It's a grub," Mr. Joshi said mildly, passing their table with a cart of returns. "It will become a beetle, if your friend stops poking it." He slid a book about garden insects onto the table without stopping, and Victoria grabbed it, because the grub had come from somewhere and she needed to know where.

"That's the thing," she said, flipping pages. "If the grub came from the fertilizer bag, then the fertilizer company shipped bugs. If it migrated over from the windowsill plants, that's different. But I can't tell, because I didn't keep anything unchanged." She stopped. "Except cup three. The control. Plain water, same dirt, same windowsill." She looked at cup three's soil. No grubs. None in cup one either, the single-fertilizer one. Two fat ones in cup two, the doubled one. "The double dose is what brought them, or what they liked. The other cups are clean."

Marek changed his mind right there, out loud. "I thought the control was a waste of a plant," he admitted. "Now it's the only reason you know anything. I'm doing one for my mold bread, too." He said it quickly, like the words cost him something, and Victoria laughed even though her best plant, the doubled one with its two fat leaves, was now the buggy one. She would have to start the trial over, and there wasn't time to grow tall beans in nine days, only short ones.

She checked out the insect book, and Mr. Joshi stamped it while telling her, unnecessarily, that beetles were faster readers than she was. At the door, Lou held cup two up to the light so they could watch a grub tunnel along the cup's edge, fat and contented, in the plant that was going to lose.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Leah had been saving for the holographic Comet Fox card for six weeks, and every night she checked the same online marketplace, BuyOrbit, where sellers posted prices and buyers snapped things up. Last month the card had sold for twelve dollars. Tonight the lowest price was thirty-five. She stared at the screen, then at her jar of allowance money, and wondered what had happened while she wasn't looking.

She scrolled through the completed sales, which the site kept in a public list. In April, eight Comet Foxes had sold, all between twelve and fifteen dollars. This week only two had appeared, and both had gone for more than thirty. There were forty-one people with the card on their wishlists. "So lots of people want it," she said to herself, "and there are almost none for sale. That's why the price shot up." She wrote the numbers in her notebook, feeling like she was mapping something invisible, like a planet you couldn't see directly but could track by the way other things moved around it.

The next morning she showed her notebook to Princeton at lunch. "Watch this," she said, pulling up her phone. "Pineberry Charms. Last winter everyone was selling them, like fifty listings, and the price dropped to two dollars each. Now there are only six listings and it's eleven dollars." Princeton squinted at the screen. "So the price isn't just... a price. It's a message about how many there are and how many people want them." Clarissa leaned over from across the table. "My brother calls that the law of demand," she said. "Price goes up, people usually buy less. Price goes down, they buy more. Unless something else changes."

Leah tested it that weekend. She found a seller with three Comet Foxes at thirty-five dollars each; the listing sat unsold for two days. Then a collector posted nine of them at once, and Leah watched the prices tumble, seller by seller, down to eighteen. Her finger hovered over the buy button. If she waited, would it fall further, or would the nine sell out and send it soaring again? She remembered Clarissa's line and decided the falling price meant people weren't buying, which meant sellers were getting nervous.

She clicked buy at seventeen dollars. Then she had an idea and checked the wishlists again: three of the nine cards were gone, and the remaining ones had already climbed to twenty-two. Her motive for waiting so long finally paid off, though she wondered whether she'd simply been lucky rather than clever. When the card arrived on Tuesday, she held it up to the window so the fox's tail caught the light.

"Eighteen dollars cheaper than the girl who bought hers on Friday," she told Princeton, sliding the card into a protective sleeve.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R.
story:
Piper laced her skates at the rental counter and read the note from Scarlette for the third time. Scarlette had written it in art class and folded it into a paper triangle: "Dmitri is taking you to the movies after the skate session, right? He says you two can get into Skull Lake because it's PG-13 and you're both twelve. My brother says Skull Lake is rated R. Check before you pay. S." Piper put the note in her jacket pocket. Dmitri was already out on the floor, wobbling near the bleachers, and she had until the session ended to sort out which movie they were actually allowed to see.

She skated a slow lap while she digested the problem. The theater's website, which she had checked on her phone in the car, listed Skull Lake as R. Dmitri insisted the poster in the lobby said PG-13. Both could not be right, and she could not see the poster from here, so she had to reason it out some other way. She thought about Scarlette's brother, who worked at the theater on weekends and had no reason to lie.

She found Ms. Müller, the rink manager, at the snack bar counting quarters. "Can I ask you a weird question?" Piper said. "You used to work at the movie theater, right? Do ratings ever change after a movie comes out?"

"Sometimes, for re-releases," Ms. Müller said. She stacked the quarters in rolls. "Why?"

"Because of Skull Lake. It came out last month, and one place says R and another says PG-13. That's an anomaly. It can't be both."

Ms. Müller frowned. "Or somebody misread the poster. What's the movie on the poster next to it?"

Piper stopped. The theater was running a summer classics series, and Scarlette's note mentioned it: Gremlins, Temple of Doom, old stuff from 1984. She pulled the note out and checked the date Scarlette had copied from the marquee. Temple of Doom, May 1984. Skull Lake, last month. Two different movies, two posters, side by side.

"PG-13 started July 1, 1984," Ms. Müller said, sliding a roll of quarters into the drawer. "Right here in the United States, as a step between PG and R. Before that date, nothing had it. So if the poster says PG-13, check which title it's under."

Piper skated back to the bench and wrote her test in the margin of Scarlette's note: if Dmitri saw PG-13 on a poster for a 1984 movie, he saw a re-release poster, not Skull Lake. When the session ended, she walked with Dmitri to the theater and stood in front of the lobby. The PG-13 poster was for the Gremlins re-release. Skull Lake, one poster over, said R in a red box the size of a dinner plate.

"So we can't see it," Dmitri said.

"We can see Gremlins," Piper said. She bought two tickets and handed him one. The rumor about her being too young for a real date had already started spreading through school, and it was corrosive, but she figured the fastest way to kill it was to walk in anyway. She pushed open the theater door and held it for him.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Xavier stood in Gael's kitchen with a plastic bag of glow stick bracelets in front of him, fifty of them, bought for the eighth grade dance that started in two hours. Gunnar picked one up, snapped it, and shook it like a thermometer until it glowed green.

"Where's the light even coming from?" Gunnar said. "There's no battery in this thing. I checked."

Xavier turned a bracelet over in his fingers. Last summer, at his little cousin's birthday party, he had bent a glow stick and felt a tiny crunch inside, like a seed shell breaking. At the time he thought nothing of it. But standing here, he remembered the crunch, and it seemed logical that the snap and the light were connected, because nothing glowed until after the snap.

"Okay, new theory," he said. "When you bend it, you break a little glass vial of hydrogen peroxide that's sealed inside. It mixes with other chemicals and a dye that are also in there. The reaction is called chemiluminescence."

Gunnar stared at him. "You made half of that up."

"I'm not sure I'm right," Xavier admitted. "My math tutor is always telling me to check my work instead of guessing, so." He held up two bracelets. "Test. We snap this one." He cracked the first bracelet and shook it. It flared orange. He held the second one up, unbroken, and they both looked at it in the dim kitchen. "And this one, we don't snap. If the light needs the vial breaking, this one stays dark no matter how long we shake it."

Gunnar took the unbroken bracelet and shook it, banged it on the counter, and rolled it under his palm like a lump of dough. It stayed as dull as a plastic straw. He shook it for a full minute, scowling harder the whole time, until the neighbor, Ms. Tse, knocked on the screen door to return a casserole dish and found Gunnar violently assaulting a bracelet on Gael's counter.

"Should I come back later?" Ms. Tse asked.

"We're doing science," Gael said solemnly, snapping another bracelet to hand to her. "Here, participation trophy."

Ms. Tse clipped the orange bracelet on her wrist, said the dish was still warm, and left through the gate with a small glowing band around her wrist, which Xavier found funnier than he could explain.

"So it works," Gunnar said. "But what if we cracked one and then didn't shake it? Would it still glow?"

"Half glow, maybe," Xavier said, and had to revise that immediately, because when they snapped a bracelet and held it dead still, only the bend point lit up, a single bright band across the middle of the tube, and the glow crept outward from there as the chemicals soaked along the plastic. "Okay, it spreads from where you break it. That actually fits. The stuff leaks out of the vial and has to travel."

Gael dumped all fifty bracelets into a mixing bowl. "Enough testing. The dance is in ninety minutes and we have to crack all of these for the eighth grade before we go." The three of them worked down the row, snap, shake, toss, snap, shake, toss, and the bowl filled up like soup made of light.

At the gym, Xavier cracked one more bracelet behind his back and handed it to the first kid he saw staring at the glowing bowl, and the kid said, "How is it doing that?" and Xavier said, "Snap it and find out."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20; both describe the same eyesight.
story:
Alexis kept the new glasses in their case all morning, snapping it open and shut under her desk until Ms. Chowdhury gave her a look. At recess she finally carried the case out to the playground, where Trey was waiting by the dilapidated climbing frame with its peeling paint and one missing rung. She had wanted glasses for a whole year, ever since she could no longer read the board, and she had a plan for this moment.

"Put them on," Trey said. "Or are you saving them for your memoir?"

"Very funny." But she was saving them, a little. Last night her cousin Devi had video-called from Manchester, and when Alexis complained about needing glasses, Devi had shrugged and said, "Mine are 6/6, so I'm fine." Alexis had stared at that sentence in the chat for an hour afterward. 6/6 sounded low and slow, like getting a six out of twenty on a quiz. Something had to be wrong with Devi's eyes, or with the numbers, and Alexis meant to figure out which before she told anyone her own score.

She opened the case and put the glasses on, and the playground snapped into focus so sharply that she flinched. The chain-link fence had individual wires. The basketball hoop had a net. Elisha came jogging over from the court, and Alexis could see her expression from thirty feet away, which had never once happened before.

"You look different," Elisha said. "Smarter? No. Just, awake."

"Listen," Alexis said. "The eye doctor wrote on my paper that I used to be 20/200 and now I'm 20/20 with the glasses. But Devi says in her country normal is 6/6. So either her eyes are way worse than mine, or..." She trailed off, because the pieces were already shifting. Devi read constantly. Devi spotted typos in group chats. "Her country uses metres," Alexis said slowly. "So the numbers on the chart are different, but the eyes are the same. 6/6 and 20/20 are the same eyesight."

Trey frowned. "That can't be. Twenty is bigger than six."

"Twenty what, though? Feet, probably. And six metres is about the same distance." She hadn't meant to test it, but the climbing frame was right there, and the eye chart sticker someone had slapped on its side years ago was still legible. She walked to the far fence, turned, and read the smallest line. Then she paced it off in steps, about twenty of them, and did the arithmetic twice in her head. Elisha watched her the whole time, arms crossed, like she was monitoring an experiment that might explode.

"Same line from both distances?" Elisha asked.

"Close enough." Alexis took the glasses off, and the chart went soft again, the playground sliding back into its old blur. She would have to tell Devi her fears had been silly, and she found she didn't mind admitting that at all. She put the glasses back on, hooked the case onto her backpack, and started toward the court, bouncing the ball Trey tossed her without breaking stride.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
The food court at the cultural festival smelled like fried plantains and cardamom, and Aubrey pushed through the crowd with her phone in one hand and a folded paper in the other. On the paper was Surah Al-Fatiha, seven lines of Arabic she was supposed to recite from memory at her coming-of-age ceremony in three weeks. She could read it fine. Reciting it was the problem, because every time she opened her eyes the words scattered like beads off a broken bracelet.

She found her cousin Yusuf at the community booth, stacking flyers about evening Quran classes. Behind him, Amaya was arranging a display of calligraphy prints, angling one frame toward the light. "Amaya wants to sell three prints today," Yusuf whispered, "so tell her you love the blue one." Amaya shot him a look, but she was already straightening the blue frame a second time, which meant he was right.

Aubrey unfolded her paper. "Will you listen to me one more time? I keep getting stuck at the fourth line." She recited, halting, then stopped and stared at the page as if it had betrayed her. "Maybe I just can't do memorization. Maybe my brain doesn't accommodate Arabic."

Yusuf laughed and held out his hand for the paper. When she gave it up, he closed his eyes and began to recite, not just her surah but chapter after chapter after chapter, his voice rising and falling like a song, on and on while the crowd noise seemed to lean away from him. Amaya abandoned her display entirely and stood listening with her mouth open. Aubrey counted on her fingers until she ran out of fingers and started over.

"How much of that do you know?" she finally interrupted.

"All of it," he said, opening his eyes. "Every one of the 114 chapters. When you finish, they call you a hafiz."

"Then you're done," Aubrey said. "Lucky."

"I recite for two hours every morning," he said, "because it slips if I don't. Keeping it perfect takes constant practice. That's the actual work." He tapped her folded paper. "You're not behind. You're just at the beginning of the same road."

Aubrey looked at her paper, then at the crowd, then made a decision that felt bigger than it was. She handed the paper to Amaya. "Hide this somewhere. I don't care where." Amaya grinned and buried it under the calligraphy prints, right beneath the blue one, which Yusuf immediately pointed at and called "the best print here," subjective as anything but clearly effective, because a woman in a green scarf picked it up two minutes later.

Standing in the noisy food court with nothing to read from, Aubrey closed her eyes. The lines came slowly, then steadily, then all seven without a single stumble. When she finished, Amaya clapped, Yusuf said "again," and she took a breath and began.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
The school was retiring its old photo board that week, and Ms. Sharma had promised that the best picture from the class would take its place in the front hall. Sadie wanted that spot. She had taken a selfie on her front porch that morning, with the sunlight just right, and she was about to post it to the class account when her thumb stopped above the button.

She zoomed in. Behind her shoulder, small but perfectly readable, sat the brass numbers nailed beside her door. Anyone looking at the photo could read her house number, and beyond it the street sign at the corner, half hidden by the hedge. Sadie sat back. She had never thought about what a photo showed besides its subject.

She decided to test the idea before she trusted it. At lunch she found Angel, who had posted a picture of herself in front of a mystery building yesterday, and Sadie studied it like a detective. There was a faded letter board, a cracked step, and one clear clue: a school logo on a gym bag in the corner, belonging to the dilapidated old middle school across town. "You can tell where this was taken," Sadie said, turning the phone around. Angel leaned close. "From a gym bag? Huh. I never noticed the bag at all."

Gordon wandered over and squinted at the picture too. "So the background is basically a map," he said. Sadie nodded, then told them about her own selfie, the numbers, the street sign. Angel had the grace to look worried for her, and Sadie appreciated that small flash of empathy. Together they worked out a fix: crop, angle, and check twice. Gordon suggested taking the new picture against the brick wall by the gym, where nothing identifiable showed.

After school Sadie took the photo again, flat against blank brick, and posted it. Ms. Sharma chose it two days later, and it went up in the front hall, big and bright, with no house number and no street sign anywhere in frame. Sadie stood admiring it when Angel tapped her shoulder and pointed at the shiny plaque beside the frame, which read, in neat letters, the name of Sadie's own school and, underneath it, the name of the photographer and her homeroom number.

"Well," Gordon said, grinning, "the wall had a sign after all."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
The tug-of-war rope lay coiled in the grass at Riverside Park like a sleeping snake, and Antoine stared at it with his arms crossed. For the third practice in a row, the coach had split them into teams and shouted the same complaint afterward: "You're easing off! Eight of you together pull like four!"

"I wasn't easing off," Ulysse muttered beside him. "Were you?"

"No," Antoine said. But he wasn't sure. When the whole team heaved at once, it was impossible to tell whose pull was real and whose wasn't. That was the thing that bothered him. Something invisible was happening inside that rope.

He borrowed a spring scale from Ms. Reyes after school. She handed it over with a raised eyebrow, and he promised to return it by Friday. At the next practice, he tied a loop of rope to a fence post, clipped the scale between the loop and the pulling rope, and asked Ulysse to pull alone. The needle jumped and settled. "Two hundred," Antoine read. Then Alana pulled alone. Two hundred ten. One at a time, every single teammate pulled alone, and every reading landed near two hundred.

"Okay," Antoine said. "Now four of you together." Ulysse, Alana, and two others heaved on the rope, and Antoine crouched to watch the needle. It climbed, but not to eight hundred. It stopped near six hundred. He made them try again with eight, and with the whole team. He wrote each number in his notebook, and the pattern stared back at him: the more people on the rope, the smaller the average pull for each one. Alone, Alana could pull two hundred ten. In a group of twelve, her share worked out to barely more than half that.

"Nobody's faking it," Antoine told the team afterward, holding up the notebook. "It just happens. I looked it up. In 1913, Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller." Alana squinted at his numbers, then at the scale still clipped to the fence.

"So how do we win Saturday?" she asked.

"We stop being a crowd." Antoine tore a page from his notebook, wrote every name on it, and held it up. "We vote by secret ballot. Whoever gets picked calls the count. One voice, one rhythm. Pull on the count, not on the guess."

Some of the older players wanted to rebel, grumbling that a seventh grader wasn't going to redesign the team. The coach let them argue for exactly ten seconds, then pointed at the fence post. "Show me."

Eight of them lined up. Ulysse took the clipboard and called, "One, two, pull." The needle shot upward, the fence post groaned, and the whole line staggered backward with the suddenness of it. Antoine looked at the scale, then at the torn ballot page fluttering in Ulysse's fist.

"Again," Alana said, gripping the rope. "One, two, pull."

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: English verbs have no future ending; English shows the future with helper words such as "will" or "going to" placed before the verb.
story:
Ms. Rivera clapped her hands twice and held up a strip of paper with Spanish words marching across it. "Next year," she announced. "That's your topic. One paragraph, in Spanish, all about your plans for next year. Future tense only." The room buzzed like a vending machine about to drop something good.

Lincoln slid his desk next to Garrett's, because Ms. Rivera had paired them for drafting. Garrett was already writing, his pencil squeaking. "Voy a donar comida," he read out loud. "I'm going to donate canned goods to the food bank next spring. That's one plan. What's yours?"

Lincoln stared at his blank paper. The marker smell from the whiteboard was sharp in his nose, and the radiator clanked its ominous warning that October had arrived. He wanted to write about the eighth-grade scavenger hunt the student council was planning, the big one where teams raced through the whole building collecting clues. But first he had to get the verbs right.

"Wait," he said, tapping his pencil. "In Spanish you stick an ending on the verb. Hablar becomes hablaré. The ending means later, next year." He wrote both forms in the margin. "So what's the English ending for that?"

Garrett squinted at his draft, which was half English, half Spanish. "I don't know. We just say it." He said his sentence out loud slowly, listening to himself. "I will donate. I am going to donate. Where's the ending?"

Courtney leaned over from the next row of desks, unable to resist a mystery. "Try one," she dared him. "Future of 'run.'"

Lincoln tested it, whispering. "I will run. I runned tomorrow? No. I run tomorrow? No." He grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote sentence after sentence, saying each one aloud like a scientist dropping chemicals into a beaker. "I will eat. I will jump. I am going to swim." Every time, the verb just sat there, unchanged. The future part came from somewhere else entirely, words parked in front of the verb like luggage loaded before a trip.

"There is no future ending in English," Lincoln said, sitting back so fast his chair scraped the floor. "English uses helper words. 'Will.' 'Going to.' They go before the verb." He counted on his fingers to be sure. One, two helper words, always in front.

Garrett slapped the desk. "So Spanish puts the future on the end, and English puts it at the front. My whole paragraph just got easier." He started copying his draft onto clean paper, fast.

Ms. Rivera wandered past their desks, raised her eyebrows at the scrap paper covered with wills and going tos, and said nothing. Lincoln grinned and wrote his first sentence in careful Spanish letters: El año que viene, voy a participar en la búsqueda del tesoro. Then, underneath, he translated it for himself: Next year, I am going to join the scavenger hunt.

"Read me the next one," Garrett begged, pencil hovering.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
story:
Edouard had blamed the blurry problem on everything except his eyes. He had blamed his desk lamp, his sleepy mornings, even Finnley, who supposedly waved at him from across the street and then, when Edouard didn't wave back, called him stuck up for a week. But when Ms. Zhao wrote the homework on the board and he copied half of it wrong, and his mother squinted at his notebook and then at him, the truth was hard to dodge. On Saturday they came home from the optometrist with a slim case in his pocket, and inside it, his first pair of glasses.

He sat on the front steps and turned the case over a few times before opening it. His objective was simple: read the street sign at the corner, the one he had been guessing at for months. Without the glasses, the sign was a gray smudge with maybe four letters. He slid the frames on, reached up to adjust the nose pads the way the optometrist had shown him, and the smudge snapped into sharp black letters. Maple Street. He laughed out loud, alone on the steps, feeling a little foolish and a lot relieved.

Archer came by on his bike, skidded to a stop, and stared. "You got glasses." He dropped onto the step beside Edouard and tried them on himself, blinking at the world gone wobbly. "Everything's huge. Whoa. Hey, how did people even read before these existed? Like, a thousand years ago, everybody just squinting forever?" Edouard started to say he had no idea, then remembered the poster in the optometrist's waiting room, the one he'd actually been able to read while he waited, about old inventions. "Glasses aren't that old," he said. "The earliest ones were made in central Italy, around 1290. Before that, no glasses anywhere. People just managed, I guess, or didn't."

"So everyone before 1290 was walking around blind-ish," Archer said, handing the glasses back. "That's rough." Then he got quiet in a way that meant he was thinking about himself. "Maybe I should get my eyes checked too. I keep moving to the front row in class and telling people I just like it there."

Later that afternoon, Edouard ran his own small experiment. Finnley was out watering the garden across the street, and Edouard had spent months assuming Finnley's silence was an insult. He stepped to the curb, lifted his hand, and waved big. Finnley's head came up, the hose swung, and the wave came back before the water soaked them both. "I thought you hated me," Finnley called. "I thought you hated me," Edouard called back, and the whole thing felt ridiculous and warm at once.

That evening Ms. Zhao from next door was collecting her mail, and she spotted the new frames. "Very handsome," she said. "How's the world looking?" Edouard considered the question. "Clearer," he said. "A little less ambiguous, anyway." He tapped the corner of his glasses and grinned at her. "Turns out the problem was never the world. I just needed these."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Empty cells in the column being grouped appear in an Excel pivot table as their own group labelled '(blank)'.
story:
The survey had been Marianna's idea, and now it was Joseph's problem. Three hundred students had answered the question "Should the cafeteria stay open during fourth period?", and Mr. Eze wanted a summary by grade, meaning Joseph had to wrestle a spreadsheet full of raw answers into something readable. He had postponed it all week, and now the presentation was due tomorrow morning.

He dragged the response column into the rows area and the grade column across the top, and the pivot table snapped together like magic. Freshmen, sophomores, juniors, seniors, each with yes and no counts branching underneath. Then his eye caught a fifth column, wedged between freshman and sophomore, labelled "(blank)". He counted its cells. Forty-two students in a grade that did not exist.

"Dante," he said across the lab table, "what grade is blank?"

Dante leaned over. "That's not a grade. That's what Excel puts there when the cell you grouped by is empty. Blank cells get their own group."

Joseph stared at the column. So somewhere in his data, forty-two rows had nothing in the grade column. But which rows, and why? He tried filtering the sheet for blanks and got an error, because some cells contained spaces, not true empties. The pattern was hidden, and hidden things bothered him. He copied the grade column into a scratch area and sorted it, watching the blank-looking cells clump together at the bottom, forty-two of them.

Then he cross-checked against the survey forms. One by one, he matched the strange rows to paper answers. Every single one belonged to a student who had answered the yes-or-no question but skipped the grade box at the top of the page. He pulled up Marissa Torres's form, then Evan Park's, then two more, and the testimony was consistent. Nobody was mysterious. Nobody was in a secret grade. They had just rushed past the first question.

He clicked back to the pivot table and wondered whether to fix the data or to say something about it. In the end he kept the "(blank)" column and made it part of the talk. He would tell the student council that forty-two people cared enough to vote but not enough to say who they were, and that they should put the grade question at the end, where people actually read it.

At the front of the room the next morning, he clicked to his last slide and pointed at the blank column with genuine curiosity. "So we asked what grade you're in," he said, "and forty-two of you answered the important question but left that one out."

A hand went up in the second row. It was Dante.

"I left it blank," Dante announced, "because the form didn't have a column for seventh grade, and I'm helping my little brother's class fill these out."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Sara had borrowed Ms. Kang's microscope on Monday, carried it home like a birthday cake, and by Wednesday she still had nothing to show for it. The assignment was due Friday: draw onion cells and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Robyn had already texted her a photo of a finished drawing, smug and detailed, and the class was holding a ballot on Friday for the best lab sketch to hang on the wall. Sara wanted her name on that wall.

She cut a chunk of onion, laid it on a slide, and pressed her eye to the lens. Darkness. Not dim, not blurry, just dark, as if she had pointed the microscope at the inside of a shoe. She tried the thick end of the slice. She tried the middle. She adjusted the mirror, then the light, then the mirror again, and the result continued to contradict every diagram in the textbook, which showed cells as neat brick walls of pale rectangles. Those diagrams clearly had not met her onion.

Alessandro came over after school, sniffed the air in the doorway, and said, "Your whole house smells like a diner." He peered into the eyepiece, squinted at the black nothing, and suggested the microscope was broken. Sara didn't think so. She held the onion chunk up to the window lamp, and the light didn't pass through it at all; the thing was a solid white wall of vegetable. Then she peeled it apart, layer by layer, until she found the papery skin inside, the thin film that clings between the rings. She held that up to the lamp and the light went straight through it, faintly amber.

"The thin inner skin is only one cell thick," she said, mostly to herself, and Alessandro said, "Meaning what?" She dropped a piece of the inner skin onto a slide with a drop of water and a whisper of iodine from the little bottle marked corrosive, which she handled with the respect it deserved, and clamped on the cover slip.

Cells. Rows and rows of them, pale rectangles with walls like drawn lines, and inside each one a dark dot sitting where the nucleus should be. Sara drew for an hour while Alessandro narrated, badly. On Friday the ballot box went around, and Ms. Kang counted the slips at the front table. "Three for this one, five for this, and one vote for a drawing of what appears to be a shoe." Sara's drawing went up on the wall by the window, second place, and she decided that was fine. Robyn could keep first. Second place still faced the light.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, so each element has one more proton than the element before it.
story:
Noah had spent eleven dollars of his allowance on a periodic table poster the size of a beach towel, and now it hung behind his volcano at the science fair like the world's most educational shower curtain.

Kylee stood next to her own project, a solar oven, and squinted at the poster across the gym. "Why does yours have numbers on it that just count up? One, two, three. That seems too easy for a science fair."

"That's not the project," Noah said. "The project is the volcano. The poster is decoration." He resented having to explain this, since the poster was clearly the best part of the table and everyone knew it.

Emmanuel wandered over from the robotics table, eating a pretzel with the seriousness of a judge. He traced a finger along the top row of elements. "Hydrogen, one. Helium, two. Lithium, three. It goes up by one the whole way." He dragged his finger down to the bottom. "Even the weird ones down here. Eighty-seven, eighty-eight, eighty-nine."

Noah looked at the poster. Emmanuel was right, and that bothered him, because the poster was supposed to be furniture, not a puzzle. "Maybe the numbers mean how heavy it is," he said.

"That's ambiguous," said Emmanuel. "Heavy like one atom of it, or heavy like a chunk you could drop on your foot?"

The gym buzzed around them. Somewhere a baking-soda volcano, not Noah's, erupted to scattered applause. Noah ignored it, which took effort. He leaned closer to the poster. The numbers counted up by one, left to right, row after row, all the way to a hundred and eighteen at the end. It was like a hidden staircase.

"So it's not weight," Noah said slowly. "It's counting something. Something you can't see."

"What can't you see in an atom?" Kylee asked.

Noah found the answer on the little box for carbon, where the poster said atomic number: 6. He checked the box next to it, nitrogen, atomic number 7. Each element had one more proton than the one before it, which meant the whole table was just elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number, all the way up. "The numbers are counting protons," he said. "Carbon has six. Nitrogen has seven. The table is counting them out in order."

"So to find how many protons an element has," Kylee said, "you just read its atomic number off the box."

"Which is why it's called the atomic number," Noah said, "and not the heavy number."

Emmanuel wrote it all down on a napkin. Ms. Nikolaidis, the judge, arrived at Noah's table with a clipboard, glanced at the volcano, and then stood in front of the poster for a long moment. "Your entry form says volcano," she said.

"The volcano is an illusion," Noah said. "It's a model of something nobody can watch happen. So is the poster. I just didn't know that an hour ago."

Ms. Nikolaidis wrote something on her clipboard that Noah couldn't see, then moved on to the solar oven. Kylee leaned over. "What did she write?"

Noah watched her go, then looked back at his poster, at carbon's little box with its six. "No idea," he said. "But I know what's in the box."

"Six protons," said Emmanuel, and ate the rest of the pretzel.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
The group chat lit up at 8:47 on Tuesday night. "Project due Thursday," Bria typed. "We still don't have a topic." Sophie stared at her phone, then at the article Mr. Paquette had handed back to her after class, the one about a new medicine tested on two thousand people. She screenshotted the headline and dropped it into the chat. "What about this? Half got the medicine, half got a placebo pill."

Nixon answered first. "Weird that they made people take fake pills. Why not just let everyone who wanted the medicine take it? Volunteers could pick." Sophie typed "idk" and then stopped, thumb hovering. It seemed like a fair question, and the guilt of having skimmed the article instead of reading it made her go back to the full text. She scrolled until she found the methods section, which usually intimidated her with its long words, but this part was short: participants were assigned to the two groups at random, by a computer.

"Found it," she wrote. "They didn't let people choose. The computer split them at random." She copied the sentence into the chat. Nixon replied with a single question mark, so Sophie read the line again, slower this time. If people picked their own group, the ones who chose the medicine might be the ones who already felt healthier, or the ones who believed in it, and that would muddy the results. "It's like drawing names out of a hat," she typed. "Random means old people and young people and sick people and healthy people get spread across both groups evenly, so the groups match."

Bria sent a thumbs up. "So the medicine group and the fake pill group start out the same. Then if the medicine group does better, it's the medicine, not the group." Sophie nodded at her screen even though nobody could see her. She opened their shared document and started the slide: "What counts as evidence?" Under it she wrote two columns. One was the two-thousand-person study with its random groups. The other was a video she'd found of a man named Tom who said the medicine had cured his knee pain in a week, all by itself.

"Is Tom wrong?" Nixon asked. Sophie thought about how to answer without making him feel dumb. "Not wrong," she typed. "But it's one person. Maybe his knee would have gotten better anyway. His story is real, but it's subjective, it's just what happened to him. The study tested it on everybody at once." Bria added, "So we put both on the slide and say which one we'd trust for our grandma." Nixon sent "ok that's actually good" and pasted the drawing-names-out-of-a-hat line into the slides. Sophie set her phone down at 9:31, opened her textbook, and underlined the word random three times.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
Chase set the microscope on the picnic table in his backyard and squinted at the sky. Ms. Charles had lent it to him until six o'clock, no later, because she needed it for her garden club meeting. That gave him three hours to learn something he was supposed to already know for Monday's quiz: how to find and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus in an onion cell.

He had forgotten to take his lab book home, so he texted Iyad. "Send me a picture of the onion slide diagram from class?" Ten minutes later his phone buzzed with a photo of the whiteboard. Iyad had added a message: "Eliot says the nucleus is easy, it's the dark blob. The other two are the tricky ones. Persevere, that's all I got."

Chase had brought the onion from the kitchen and a small knife. He cut the onion in half, peeled one of the curved layers apart, and tugged off a thin, transparent strip of skin from the inside surface with tweezers. He laid the strip in a drop of water on a slide, dropped the cover slip over it, and clipped it onto the stage. The first thing he noticed was that his eyes stung from the onion juice, which Iyad had warned him about and which he had ignored.

At forty times magnification he saw mostly a pale blur. He turned the knob to one hundred, adjusted the focus, and sat back. What filled the circle of light looked like a brick wall. Straight rows of flattened rectangles, packed together, each one bordered by a dark, thick line. He actually laughed out loud. "I grew a brick wall in a drop of water," he said to nobody.

Then he stopped laughing and frowned at it. A brick wall would be made of many bricks. But his diagram from Iyad's photo showed a few cells, and each cell was drawn as a bordered box. He looked again at the rows in the eyepiece. Each rectangle had its own thick outer border, and inside each one, faint near the edge, was an even thinner line hugging that border. The thick dark boundary was the cell wall, and the fine line just inside it had to be the membrane. Near the center of one rectangle sat a small dark blob, exactly as Eliot had described the nucleus. The wall was what made the cells look like rows of bricks, but the bricks themselves were the cells, one single cell per brick.

Chase drew what he saw in his notebook, labeling the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus, then drew a second one at higher magnification to check himself. The blob stayed in the same place. The thin inner line stayed put when he tapped the slide and everything shifted together. He texted Eliot a photo of his drawing. "The brick wall thing. Each brick is one cell, right?" Eliot replied with a thumbs up and one word: "Yep."

At five thirty he wiped the lenses with the cloth Ms. Charles had given him and carried the microscope next door. She was watering a planter of tropical flowers by her porch, and a bee was working its way across them, after the nectar in each bloom. "Did you find what you needed?" she asked. "The onion, I mean."

"Found a brick wall first," Chase said, "and then I found out it wasn't one." He handed her the microscope and turned back toward his yard, still carrying his notebook with the two drawings open to the page.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Active listening means giving someone full attention and then showing you heard them, for example by asking a follow-up question about what they said.
story:
Sebastian got to the park fifteen minutes early, which gave him time to check the drone battery twice. Full voltage, all four lights green. He had packed the frisbee too, because frisbees are versatile; you can throw it, sit on it, or use it as a plate, and he wanted options in case the conversation ran out.

Alessia arrived on her bike at exactly two o'clock. "Hi," she said. "Nice drone."

"Thanks, it's my uncle's," Sebastian said, and then he talked. He talked about the drone's three flight modes. He talked about how he had built a birdhouse last summer. He talked about the book he was reading, the video game he had beaten, and the time he and Adam found a wasp nest trying to colonize the old hollow tree by the creek. Alessia walked beside him and nodded, and said "cool" twice, and once "wow," and Sebastian kept going because silence felt like falling.

They stopped at the picnic tables near the duck pond, where ants had colonized a spilled ice cream cone, marching in a neat brown line. Alessia was watching them, and Sebastian realized he did not know what she had been doing all week, or whether she liked drones, or anything about her at all. He remembered what Adam had told him on Friday. "You have to do active listening," Adam had said, shaking his head. "Not just nodding while you plan your next sentence."

Sebastian picked up the frisbee, then set it down again and turned so he was facing her, phone still in his pocket where it belonged. "You said your grandma came to visit," he said. "You never told me what she's like."

Alessia looked up from the ants. "You remembered that?" She smiled, and then she talked for the next ten minutes about her grandmother's garden, the plum tree, the cat named Turnip, and how she wanted to plant vegetables on the balcony this spring. Sebastian listened the whole time without interrupting once, and when she paused he asked what she would grow first. She said tomatoes, definitely, and asked whether he thought that was too hard for a beginner.

"Tomatoes are versatile," Sebastian said. "You can do anything with them."

Alessia laughed. "You said that word about the frisbee an hour ago."

"That's because I practiced three topics last night," he admitted, "and I got through all of them before we reached the pond."

She leaned her chin on her hand. "Funny. I practiced three too. You just never gave me a turn."

"Okay," he said, and tossed her the frisbee. "Your turn first, all four topics, go."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
Violet spread three ads across the library table: a poster for Sparkle Crunch cereal, a magazine page for tennis shoes, and a flyer for the town's new sports drink. Mr. Banerjee, the librarian, had said the winning poster for the media literacy contest would teach other students one real thing about how advertising works, and she had until Saturday to figure hers out.

Bernard dropped into the chair beside her and slid the cereal ad closer. "This one's mine. Look, it says 'all-natural goodness' right across the top. That's why my mom buys it." Violet turned the box picture over, where someone had taped a photocopy of the nutrition panel, and ran her finger down the ingredient list. Sugar, corn syrup, red dye, and a long chemical name she couldn't pronounce sat near the top.

"That doesn't sound natural," Bernard said, leaning in. "Or good." Violet tapped the phrase on the front. "But it makes you feel like it's both, and it never actually says anything you can check. My book calls that glittering generalities. Vague, positive words like 'freedom' or 'natural' that sound great but mean nothing specific." She copied the phrase onto her notepad, then flipped to the shoe ad. A famous soccer player grinned over the words "Everyone's already wearing them." Bernard shrugged. "So? If everyone wears them, they must be good."

"Or that's the trick," Violet said. "It wants you to feel left out. That's a bandwagon appeal." Jared arrived with a stack of magazines and flopped into the last chair. "There's a whole other kind in here," he said, showing a soda ad with a pop star's face filling the page. "She probably doesn't even drink it. Celebrity testimonial." He sounded proud of the words, and Violet grinned at him. "Put it on the pile. We've got a system going."

They tested each ad like an experiment. Violet covered the famous faces and the crowd photos with sticky notes and read only the plain print underneath. Time after time, nothing specific remained. The sports drink promised "pure athletic greatness" but listed no ingredient that differed from the cheaper brand beside it. Jared stood up, rolled his ankles, and pointed at his heel. "It's like when I strained my tendon and the coach made me rest to conserve my strength for the final. The real information was boring and specific. The ads are the opposite."

By closing time their poster read: Cover the famous face. Ignore the crowd. Read the back of the box. Mr. Banerjee walked past on his way to lock the display case and paused at their table. "May I?" He studied the poster for a long moment, then set it upright. "This one goes in the window," he said. "Starting tomorrow."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
The festival map was useless because Jade's booth assignment had nothing to do with her own heritage. Every volunteer had drawn a slip from a basket at the community centre, and Jade's slip said Ukrainian egg decorating, even though she had never held a wax stylus in her life. Erika had drawn West African drumming, and Sahib had drawn the Filipino dessert table, and all three of them stood under the humid tent canopy complaining about it before the gates opened.

"Maybe I can trade," Jade said. "There's a woman at my table from the weavers guild, so at least somebody there actually knows something." She watched Erika drum her fingers on a plastic bucket, clearly wishing it were a djembe. "Or maybe I just learn six eggs' worth of patterns and fake the rest."

Sahib shook his head. He wanted to win the festival's booth contest, and he had decided that winning required the dessert table to run out of nothing and burn nobody. "No trades," he said. "We got our tables by drawing names out of a basket. Totally random. That's the rule now, apparently."

By noon, the random tables had become teams. The drummers defended their shade with the fierceness of people who had earned it, the dessert table chanted Sahib's name when he found extra coconut milk in the storeroom, and Jade caught herself bragging about wax resist technique to a ten-year-old as though she had learned it from her grandmother. She paused with the stylus hovering over an egg and frowned.

"Erika," she said, when her friend wandered over between sets, "did you notice we're all acting like our tables are the best? Like, for real. Sahib called the drummers 'the loud booth' with actual venom."

Erika wiped her forehead with her wrist. "Ms. Eze was telling some parents about that this morning. She said a psychologist named Henri Tajfel did experiments where people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. She said it like it was a fun fact. I thought, that is literally us."

Jade turned the half-finished egg in her hand. So the pattern was real, and she was inside it, and so was everyone under the tent. She tried a small experiment. She walked to the drum circle and told Erika's group, out loud, that their rhythm was the best thing at the festival, and meant it, and watched the drummer in the yellow shirt immediately relax his shoulders and offer her a stool. Then she went back to her own table and heard herself say, within minutes, "Of course, eggs are harder than drumming. One slip of the wax and it's ruined." She hadn't planned to say it. It had just arrived.

She decided to revise her plan for the afternoon. Instead of defending the egg booth, she put a sign-up sheet beside the wax pots that said Learn Any Table's Craft, and the weaver from the guild, without being asked, added a line beneath it: Visitors welcome, rivals welcome, beginners welcome. By three o'clock the drummers were attempting pysanky with mixed results, and Sahib was teaching a Ukrainian grandmother how to fold turon, and the grandmother was teaching him a word for it he could not pronounce, and he tried it anyway, three times.

Jade stood at her station with the stylus warm in her hand, watching Erika carefully copy a diamond pattern onto a brown egg, and she thought about tomorrow's slips, and whether anyone would volunteer to draw a table they didn't want.

"Okay," Erika said, holding the egg up to the light, "but if mine cracks, I'm blaming your booth."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Dylan stood at the edge of the drama room with his hands in his pockets, hoping Mr. Russo would skip over him. Mr. Russo pulled a battered paperback from the props shelf, its spine held together with tape, and dropped it on the table. "This is Viola Spolin's 1963 book," he said. "It collected theater games, and people call it the bible of improv teaching." He flipped it open to a page marked with a paper clip. "Today we play one. Partners. Yes, and."

Dylan got paired with Ayoub, who grinned like this was the best news of the week. Dylan did not feel the same. He liked lines he could memorize, not scenes he had to make up on the spot.

The game seemed simple. Ayoub would start a scene with a line, and Dylan had to accept it and add something. Ayoub cleared his throat. "We're astronauts, and the ship is leaking air." Dylan froze. "No we're not," he said, and Ayoub's shoulders dropped. Mr. Russo rang a small bell. "That's a block," he called, not unkindly. "Try again."

They tried again, and again Dylan blocked. "You're holding a snake." "That's a rope." The bell rang each time, and Dylan could hear Jethro and his partner laughing across the room, building a scene about a haunted bakery that got stranger and funnier every line. Dylan started to notice a pattern: every time he said no, the scene stopped like a car hitting a wall, and every time Jethro said yes, and, the scene grew. The rule was invisible, but the evidence was all around him. He quietly made an assumption he could test: the yes was the engine, and the and was the steering wheel.

Ayoub offered him a new opening, gentler than before, as if he knew Dylan needed a smaller door to walk through. "I found a key on the gym floor." Dylan took a breath. "Yes, and it's warm, like someone was just holding it." Ayoub's face lit up. "Yes, and there's writing on it, but it's backwards." "Yes, and we need a mirror to read it." The scene rolled forward on its own, and Dylan forgot to be nervous. When they got locked in the janitor's closet by an invisible key thief, half the class was watching, and even Jethro had stopped to listen.

Afterward Mr. Russo asked Dylan what had changed. Dylan pointed at the taped-up book on the table. "That game," he said. "It illustrated something. Saying no just kills it." Mr. Russo smiled and slid the book across. "Spolin's games have been doing that since 1963. Take it home if you want." Dylan tucked it under his arm, and Ayoub fell into step beside him in the hallway. "Tomorrow," Ayoub said, "the key thief has a brother."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791.
story:
The pocket-sized booklet was wedged behind Grandma's dictionary, its cover soft from years of being carried. Georgia pulled it out and read the gold letters: The Constitution of the United States. Her presentation was Monday morning, and she had nothing yet except a printout of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a deadline that Ms. Gauthier would not move, not even for the flu going around the school.

"You find something up there?" Grandma called from the kitchen, where the kettle was already whistling even though nobody had asked for tea. That had been happening more lately, kettles and lamps and sprinklers going at odd hours.

"It was Grandpa's," Georgia said, turning the thin pages. "It has the amendments in the back." She knew some of this already from a video call with Mariah last night, because Mariah's mother had grown up in Michigan. "The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights," Mariah had said, holding up her own phone to show a photo of a classroom poster. "They were ratified in 1791. My mom made me memorize that in third grade." Georgia had written it on her hand at bedtime and copied it onto a sticky note by morning.

She spread the Charter printout beside the booklet on the kitchen table, next to Grandma's cooling tea. The two documents did not match, and that was the problem she wanted to crack. Her assignment was to pick one right and articulate it in her own words, but every time she tried, she just copied the official sentences. Ms. Gauthier had circled a whole paragraph of Georgia's draft and written, in red, "This is the right's clothing. Where is the right itself?"

Georgia tried an experiment. She chose the right against unreasonable search, which existed in both documents, and covered the printed words with her hands. Then she said it plain, out loud, to the sugar bowl: nobody can go through your stuff for no reason; they have to have a real cause. It sounded too simple. She said it again a different way: the rule is that the government has to justify itself before it touches you, not after. That one sat better in her mouth, like a stone she could hold.

"Your grandfather used to say it was a turbulent time, when they wrote those," Grandma said, sitting down across from her. "People shouting about what a new country should be allowed to do." She peered at the booklet, then at the Charter, and her brow folded. "Which one is ours?"

"Ours is the Charter," Georgia said gently. "That one was his."

"Well," Grandma said, patting the booklet's cover as though it were a cat, "he'd be glad you're reading it." She looked up at the window, where the sprinkler was running in the dark. Georgia wrote her sentence on a fresh card, folded Grandpa's booklet into her backpack, and turned off the kettle before it boiled dry.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
story:
Katherine spread the bank statement across her grandfather's kitchen table, next to the savings goal she had written on a napkin: five hundred dollars by the end of high school. The statement listed two numbers that refused to match, an interest rate and, beside it, a slightly higher figure labelled APY. "Why are there two?" she asked, tapping the paper. "Which one is mine?"

Her grandfather shrugged and went back to his coffee. "You're the one taking the math elective. You tell me." Mia, who had come along to help clean out the attic, leaned over Katherine's shoulder. "Maybe the bank made a printing error," Mia said. "Or maybe one of them is a trick." Katherine felt her whole plan hinge on the answer, because she had promised herself she would compare what her money could do over five years before she opened the account.

She fetched her notebook and worked the simple version first: five percent of two hundred dollars, added up year by year, would not accelerate anywhere exciting. Then she tried letting each year's interest join the pile before the next year was counted, and watched the total creep higher than the simple version. Not by much, but by something. When she divided to find what that worked out to per year, the answer landed almost exactly on the smaller printed number, the APY, not the interest rate. "It's not a trick," she said, half to herself.

"Prove it," Mia said, defiant on the bank's behalf, arms crossed. So Katherine looked it up on her grandfather's old laptop while he watched from his chair. The page said that under the Truth in Savings Act of 1991, banks in the United States have to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, and that the APY includes the effect of compounding. "See," Katherine said, turning the screen toward Mia. "The APY is the honest number. Compounding is already baked into it."

She copied both five-year totals into her notebook, one for simple interest and one for compounding, and drew a box around the difference. "Eleven extra dollars," she announced. "That's two sandwiches and a bus ticket, for doing nothing but leaving the money alone." Her grandfather laughed and slid his pen across the table so she could underline the winner. "Then go open the account," he said. "And put my ten dollars in with it."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
The bleachers were folded against the wall because the workers were coming to renovate the gymnasium over spring break, so the whole spelling bee audience sat in folding chairs that creaked every time someone shifted. Ella stood in line with Ashlynn and Philip, holding her number card, number fourteen, and going over the list of words she had copied from the library the night before. She had gone to the library looking for practice words and had pulled a heavy old volume off the bottom shelf instead, a copy of Samuel Johnson's "A Dictionary of the English Language." The librarian had told her it was published in 1755 and that it helped settle how many English words were spelled. Ella had sat there a long time, turning the brittle pages, thinking it was strange that spellings had ever needed settling at all, that somebody had to decide.

Now Mr. Kaur, who was running the bee, tapped the microphone. "We'll go through the lineup once, then sudden death rounds until we have a champion. You have ninety seconds per word." Ninety seconds. Ella folded her hands.

Ashlynn went out on "gregarious," missing a letter near the end. Philip survived "conscientious" by whispering it to himself twice before starting. Ella got "melancholy," and then, three rounds later, it was down to her and a boy from another class whose card said number two.

Mr. Kaur looked at his card and read, "Simile." Ella asked for the definition, and he said it was a comparison using like or as. That was easy, and she spelled it slowly, correctly, and watched the boy swallow.

His word was "abrupt." He started too fast, added a letter that didn't belong, and stopped halfway through with an abrupt silence. Ella was the champion. People clapped, Mr. Kaur handed her a small trophy, and a woman from the front row stood up to take a photo for the school website.

"Champion," the woman said, "tell us your secret. Hours of drills?"

"One night," Ella said. "I found an old dictionary."

"A spelling book?"

"Not exactly. Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language.' It was published in 1755, and it helped settle how a lot of English words were spelled." She lifted the trophy. "I figured if I knew who decided the spellings, I'd know what to expect."

Mr. Kaur was stacking his index cards at the microphone, and he cleared his throat. "Ella," he said, holding up the deck, "you should know I wrote these rounds from the modern district list. Every word you missed in practice came from that old dictionary of yours, and every word you got right was one the district added after they decided to renovate the library this summer and toss the bottom shelf." He dealt the cards onto the table like evidence. "The book you studied from is the one leaving the building."

Ella looked at the trophy, then at the door where two workers were already rolling in tarps. "Then I'd better take it home tonight," she said, and she went to pull it off the shelf before the bell.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
The farm smelled like wet hay and motor oil, which was not what Gabriella had expected from a science field trip. Ms. Fraser had set up a folding table beside the barn, and on it sat three microscopes in padded cases that had clearly cost the school a great deal of expense, because the principal had mentioned it twice during announcements. Each student had to peel a paper-thin layer off an onion from the farm's storage shed, stain it with iodine, and find the cells.

Gabriella's layer tore twice before she got a piece small enough to lie flat on the slide. Through the eyepiece, at first, she saw nothing but a pale smear. Then she turned the fine focus, and the smear broke apart into neat brick-shaped cells, row after row of them, like a wall built by someone very patient.

"There's no way this is only fifty times," Rory said from the next microscope. "My cells look bigger than my thumb."

"Fifty times," Nash said. "It says ten on the eyepiece and forty on the lens thing. Ten plus forty is fifty."

Gabriella lifted her head. "Why would you add them?"

Nash shrugged. "Because they're both magnifying."

She looked down at her own microscope. The eyepiece, the part her eye touched, had 10x printed on it in tiny silver letters. The rotating metal nosepiece held four objectives, and the one clicked into place over her slide read 40x. She thought about it while an irritated chicken paced the barn doorway, watching the class with what she could only describe as predatory attention, as if the onion slides might be edible.

"I think you multiply," she said. "Ten times forty. That's four hundred."

"You can't just decide that," Rory said.

"Watch me." Gabriella swapped to the smaller objective, the one marked 10x. Through the eyepiece the cells shrank to a faint mesh. Ten times ten would be one hundred, and one hundred looked like this. She clicked back to the 40x lens, and the brick wall swelled into place again, four times wider than before. "See? If adding were right, going from forty to ten on the objective should shrink it a little. It shrinks it a lot. Four times."

Nash checked his own eyepiece, found the same silver 10x, and said nothing for a moment. "Fine. Four hundred," he said, in the voice of someone conceding a point at the expense of his dignity.

Ms. Fraser drifted past, looked at Gabriella's slide, and raised one eyebrow. "Wall, membrane, nucleus. All three, in your sketch, before the bus leaves." She moved on without another word, which was either high praise or a threat. With Gabriella it was often hard to tell.

Gabriella bent over the eyepiece again and began to draw. The cell wall was the outer rectangle, easy. The membrane hugged it just inside, thin as a rumor. The nucleus took longer to find; she nudged the slide a fraction, and there it was, a small dark circle orbiting the middle of one cell like a moon that had decided to sit down. She labeled all three, then sat back and looked at the chicken, which was now standing directly on Nash's notebook.

"Your predator has my data," Nash said.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: To test whether n is prime, you only need to try divisors up to its square root, because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root.
story:
Colton had been typing for eleven minutes and the little cursor in the terminal just blinked at him, waiting. His program asked for a number, then divided it by 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on until it found a factor or ran out of patience. He had typed in 999,999,937, a number Maia had dared him to try, and now the computer lab smelled like thirty warm monitors and nobody was talking.

"It's frozen," said Maia, leaning over from the next seat. "Restart it."

"It's not frozen. It's thinking." Colton pointed at the fan humming inside the machine. "It's on, like, divisor forty thousand by now."

Maia did not care about divisors. Maia cared about the app she was building for the young entrepreneur contest in March, a homework tracker that buzzed at you with increasing urgency, and she needed Colton's prime checker as a small part of it, for reasons she had explained twice and he had forgotten twice. "Every second you sit here is a cumulative loss for my launch date," she said. "That's a business term."

He ignored her and stared at his loop. Divide, check, divide, check. Then he thought about what a factor actually was. If 999,999,937 was a times b, both of them couldn't be huge, because two huge numbers multiplied together would blast past 999,999,937. One of them had to be small. Small meant no bigger than the square root of 999,999,937, which was somewhere around thirty-one thousand, a number he could reach in a blink.

He cut the loop off at the square root and ran it again. The answer appeared so fast he thought he had broken something. "Prime," the terminal said, instantly, as if it had known all along and had merely been waiting for Colton to catch up. Maia refused to believe it. "That can't be right. It just skipped a million numbers." So he tried to refute it himself, typing in 999,999,929, and the program printed "divisible by 9401" just as fast, which meant the short loop was really checking, not guessing.

"That's actually useful," Maia admitted, already sketching a buzz schedule on her notebook cover. "Fast prime checks, that's a selling point. I'm putting you in the credits."

Ms. Santoso came around the lab collecting the exit tickets, and stopped at Colton's screen. "Nice work. You know the assignment only asks about numbers up to a hundred, though." She smiled at his eleven-minute martyrdom on the terminal behind her, still faithfully dividing nothing.

Colton saved his file anyway. "Ms. Santoso," he said, "what's the square root of extra credit?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Jonathan had never been inside Sakura House, the little Japanese restaurant on Miller Street, and he was nervous about two things: the gift in his backpack, and the fact that Leyla's family knew exactly how to act there and he did not. Leyla's grandmother owned the place, and after weeks of Leyla tutoring him in math for free, his mom had insisted he bring something to thank her. The wrapped box of green tea had seemed like a legitimate choice at the store. Now it felt like a test he hadn't studied for.

"Grandma lives upstairs," Leyla said when they arrived, holding the side door open. "We eat in the kitchen sometimes." Jonathan stepped in and stopped. The floor just inside the door was lower than the rest, a shallow trench of tile, and a neat row of shoes sat along its edge, toes pointing out. Beyond it, the floor rose a step to a hallway carpeted in pale runners. Two pairs of guest slippers waited there, lined up like they had been expecting him.

William, who had invited himself along, walked straight past the shoes and onto the raised hallway in his sneakers. "Come on, we're late," he said. Leyla's grandmother appeared from the kitchen, and Jonathan watched her eyes drop to William's feet. She didn't say anything, but her smile went thin at the edges, and William suddenly seemed to notice the row of shoes behind him all at once. His ears turned red.

Jonathan tested his idea before moving. The shoes came off in the low area, so that patch must be where it happened, and the slippers must be for after. He unlaced his shoes, set them beside the row facing the door, and stepped up into the slippers. "Genkan," Leyla said quietly, nodding at the sunken tile. "That's what my grandma calls it." William backed up, nearly tripping into the trench, and switched to the other pair of slippers with the careful movements of someone dismantling a bomb.

In the apartment kitchen, Jonathan handed over the tea with both hands because that seemed safer than one. To his surprise, Leyla's grandmother did not open it. She set it on the cabinet shelf, said something warm in Japanese, and pressed a small wrapped parcel into his hands in return. He had assumed gifts got torn into right away, like at his own birthday parties, and the fact that she hadn't made him wonder if he'd picked the wrong thing. But Leyla was smiling at him, and the parcel in his hands had real weight.

Dinner was tempura and rice, and the three of them demolished it. William, who had spent the whole walk bragging about knowing chopsticks, kept dropping his shrimp; Leyla, without a word, slid the little chopstick rest toward him and demonstrated a slower grip. Jonathan noticed how her grandmother watched all of it, the dropped shrimp, the corrections, the way nobody mentioned William's earlier mistake. Then she leaned across the table and pointed her chopsticks at William's plate.

"You try," she said. "Slow is better than fast."

William looked at her for a second, then at his hands, and started over.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Parker slumped onto the bench outside the gym, holding his phone like it was evidence in a trial. Tenley had gone silent on him at lunch, and he had spent all of sixth period trying to figure out why. His best guess: she had found out that he had read her texts when she left her phone on his desk Friday. He had only meant to check the time, but one message had led to another, and now his stomach was doing that anxious flip it did before tests he hadn't studied for.

"Mr. Wright says stress lives in the body," said Subhan, dropping down beside him and offering half a granola bar. "That's why your face looks like that. So, what did you do?"

"I don't know yet. That's the problem." Parker took the granola bar anyway, because eating something was his mom's coping trick and it sometimes worked. "She was fine Friday morning. She was weird Friday after school. Something happened in between, and I was with her the whole time except for the phone thing."

Subhan raised an eyebrow. "The phone thing."

"Okay, the phone thing might be the hidden cause. But here's my test. If she's mad about the phone, she'll still be mad today but not mad at you. If she's mad about something else, like the canceled trip, she'll be mad at everyone. So go say hi and report back."

"You want me to be your lab rat." Subhan stood up anyway, brushing crumbs off his jeans. "If I get excluded from the group chat because of this, you owe me lunch for a week."

Tenley was at her locker, and Parker watched from the bench like a detective who had accidentally made himself the suspect. She said hi to Subhan. Then she said something longer, glancing toward Parker, and Subhan walked back slowly, like a man approaching a dragon, or worse, a girl with a grievance.

"She says you read her messages," he reported. "Also, and I quote, tell him I'm not an adversary, this isn't a duel, I just want him to understand."

Parker crossed the hallway. His mouth was dry, and his heart was doing a rhythm that would have impressed the band teacher. "I did read them. I'm sorry. I should have asked first."
