"Yeah, you should have." Tenley shut her locker. "It's about boundaries. A boundary is a limit I set about what I'm comfortable with, like how people treat me, touch me, or use my stuff. My phone, my bag, my journal. You ask first, even for the time."

"So it's not that you hate me."

"It's that you crossed a line without noticing there was a line." She almost smiled. "There was a very clear line, Parker. It had, like, seventeen flags on it."

He held up both hands. "No flags crossed from now on. I'll ask before I even look at your pencil case. I'll send a formal request in writing. I'll get it notarized."

"That's a lot of paperwork for a pencil."

"I'm thorough."

Tenley laughed then, the real kind, and Subhan, who had crept closer pretending to check the lost-and-found board, gave a spontaneous round of applause that made a passing sixth grader join in for no reason at all.

"Tomorrow, bring your phone to lunch," Tenley said, slinging her backpack over one shoulder. "I'll set a password you can't guess, and we'll test whether you've really learned self-control."

"It'll be the easiest test of my life," Parker said. "Except for the time I sneezed during the fire drill."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law.
story:
The beach at Yellowstone Lake was nothing like the ocean beach back home, but Lily spread her towel on the gray sand anyway and dared her brother to stick a toe in the water. He yelped. She laughed. Their parents were still unloading the cooler, and her friends Maika and Rylen, whose family had come on the trip with them, were trying to salvage their sandwiches from a raiding band of gulls. "Sophisticated birds," Rylen said, shaking out a bag of chips the gulls had opened with two precise jabs. "They wait until you look away."

That night there was a campfire talk at the amphitheater, and the park ranger, Mr. Berg, walked the rows of folding chairs with a microphone asking questions. He handed out Junior Ranger badges for correct answers, and Lily wanted one badly. She had answered three questions right already, from the booklet she'd read in the car. Then Mr. Berg asked one that emptied every raised hand in the crowd. "What was the first national park in the United States, on what date did it become one, and which president signed it into law?" Her parents guessed Yosemite. Maika's parents guessed the Grand Canyon. Rylen whispered something about Abraham Lincoln. Nobody got it, and Mr. Berg moved on without telling them, which Lily thought was almost mean.

She couldn't stop turning it over on the walk back to the tent. The answer was hiding somewhere, she figured, the same way the gulls' plan had been hidden until they struck. Parks put their own history on display. That was a rule she could test. So the next morning, while everyone else slept, she took the flashlight and walked to the visitor center, which opened early, and went plaque by plaque along the stone arch outside.

The big bronze plaque near the door read like a birthday card. Established March 1, 1872. She copied it into her notebook. The park's own name was carved above the entrance, so that part was settled too, but the president was still missing. She dug the folded five-dollar bill out of her shoe, where she kept it at the beach, and smoothed it flat under the flashlight. The face on it belonged to Ulysses S. Grant. It was a guess built on a pattern, and she would have to test it out loud.

At the next campfire, Mr. Berg asked the same stumper again, and Lily's hand went up before he finished. "Yellowstone," she said. "It became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law." Mr. Berg froze with the badge halfway to her hand, then pressed it into her palm. A parliament of owls called from the pines behind the amphitheater as she sat down, and Rylen leaned over and whispered, "The five-dollar bill, wasn't it?" Lily just held the badge up so it caught the firelight.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Andrew stood on the stage in the drama room with his arms crossed, which was part of the problem. Mr. Nolan had spent two weeks teaching the class to improvise with a partner by accepting every offer with "yes, and," and Andrew still couldn't make a scene last longer than thirty seconds. Nova, his partner, would say something like, "We're lost in the woods," and Andrew would say, "Yes, and we have a map," and then the scene would just stop, like a wind-up toy that had run down.

After class he went to the school library and searched the shelf behind the biography section, where the theater books were hidden. He found a battered paperback called "Impro," written by a man named Keith Johnstone in 1979. He sat on the floor between the shelves and read the chapter about status. The book said characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama. Andrew read the sentence twice. He had never thought about a scene having levels before, like a stack of steps where somebody stood on top and somebody stood below.

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before Friday's performance. The class had been assigned a prototype scene, a simple king and servant sketch meant to teach basic structure, and Andrew's plan was rebellious in a small way: instead of keeping the king on top the whole time, the servant would start giving orders halfway through. If the book was right, the shift would make the scene come alive. If it was wrong, he would look like an idiot in front of everyone.

On Friday, Nova played the king and sat on a chair that stood in for a throne. Andrew entered with an imaginary tray. "Your soup, Your Majesty," he said, bowing so low his knees bent.

"Yes, and it's cold," Nova said, waving him away. "Take it back."

"Good, because I seasoned it myself, and you'll eat it while I take your carriage to the market." Andrew straightened up and pointed at the door. The audience, which had been silent, started laughing. Nova blinked, then leaned forward in the throne.

"Yes, and you may take the carriage," Nova said, "but the driver obeys me."

"The driver obeys me now," Andrew said. "I gave him a raise."

The laughing got louder. Mr. Nolan, who had been writing on his clipboard, looked up and did not write anything for a moment. When the scene ended, he walked over. "That was the first time your scenes didn't cease after two lines," he said. "What changed?"

Andrew held up the paperback, its cover soft from forty years of hands. "This book says shifting status creates drama."

Nova took it and flipped to the dog-eared page. "Keith Johnstone, 1979," Nova read aloud, and tapped the paragraph. "Can I borrow it after you?"

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
story:
The bleachers were half empty for the time trials, but Justin's stomach was as tight as it would be at a real meet. He had one job today: run eight hundred metres without dying in the second lap, the thing that had happened at every race since September. Mr. Nikolaidis had told them to bring a plan, and Justin's plan sat folded in his pocket like a secret.

"Remember," Fatima said, stretching beside him on the infield, "you don't have to beat Drayden today. You have to beat your old time." Drayden was already at the start line, bouncing on his toes, fast out of the blocks the way he always was. Justin had watched enough races to see a pattern in Drayden's losses too: brilliant first lap, collapse in the second. Something invisible was at work, and Justin was starting to think it could be measured.

The whistle blew. Justin hung back on purpose, letting Drayden and another boy migrate to the front while he sat third, feeling controlled, smooth, strong. Too strong, maybe. His legs felt fantastic, and the track unrolled under him so easily that he stopped counting his effort and just ran.

"Sixty-two!" Mr. Nikolaidis shouted as Justin came through the first turn of the second lap. Sixty-two. Justin's mind snagged on the number. He had planned something around seventy. He tried to remember what the coach had called the shouted time at the last meet, when a runner in the outside lane had gone out crazy fast. He hadn't asked then. He asked now, gasping as he passed the bench.

"Your split," Mr. Nikolaidis called. "One lap, sixty-two seconds."

A split was the time for one section of a race, then, one lap of it, and a runner's four-hundred-metre split showed right away whether the first lap had been faster or slower than planned. Justin's first lap had been way faster than planned. Way faster. His legs confirmed it before his brain did, flooding with heaviness exactly where the backstretch began. Drayden was ten metres ahead and wobbling, arms punching the air, slowing so visibly it looked like he was running uphill. Justin was slowing too, but less, and the gap shrank metre by metre.

He crossed the line behind Drayden and bent double, hands on knees, watching the grass blur. Fatima jogged over with her clipboard, ready to deliver her usual critique, which was blunt but fair. "You went out too hard," she said. "Sixty-two. Your plan said seventy."

"I know," Justin wheezed. "I felt great, so I forgot the plan." He straightened up and looked down the track at Drayden, who was still walking it off in small circles. Two boys, two identical mistakes, one distinct number to explain them both. "Next time," Justin said, "somebody shouts my split at the first lap, not the second. Then I can fix it while it's still fixable." He looked at Mr. Nikolaidis, who raised his stopwatch and nodded once.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Some element symbols come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.
story:
Antoine spread the periodic table across the kitchen table and held it flat with two mugs, one on each corner, because the printout refused to lie still. Ms. Liu had promised a quiz tomorrow: she would name an element, and they had to give the number of protons in its atoms. Antoine had figured out that part fairly quickly. The atomic number sat right above each symbol, and the atomic number matched the proton count, so gold, number 79, meant 79 protons. That rule felt solid. The problem was the symbols themselves, which behaved like a code written by someone who wanted to confuse him personally.

The phone buzzed. Dan had sent a photo of his own printout with the message, "Iron. Timed. Go." Antoine ran his finger down the left side of the table. He found hydrogen, lithium, sodium, all making sense. He kept going, hunting for a big capital I. There was iodine, which had apparently stolen the letter, and there was iridium, but no I standing alone for iron. He checked twice, then a third time, dragging his finger so slowly it was like trying to excavate a fossil from rock with a teaspoon.

"Twenty-six," he typed. Then, before Dan could reply, he sent another message. "Wait. I guessed. I can't find iron on this thing."

"Found it," Dan wrote back a minute later. "It's Fe. My dad says it's from Latin. Ferrum. So Fe for iron."

Antoine stared at the little square. Fe, number 26. Of course it wasn't I. Of course the table would hide iron behind a language he didn't speak. He checked the atomic number anyway, because guessing had nearly fooled him once already. Twenty-six, so 26 protons, and the answer he had blurted out out of pure luck was actually right. He laughed at himself, alone in the kitchen, which felt slightly ridiculous.

Angel texted the group next: "Is anyone else finding these symbols ambiguous? K is potassium? Who decided that?" Antoine sent back a picture of the iron square with "Fe. Ferrum. Latin. Dan's dad is a legend." Then he made himself a new game. He would call out an element, Dan and Angel would answer with the proton count, and nobody could check the table until they had committed to a number. Silver caught Angel, who said 47 after a long pause and turned out to be exactly right. Tin caught Antoine, who said 22 instead of 50, and Dan typed a single crying-laughing face at him.

By ten o'clock Antoine had gone through the whole table twice, and the once-impossible squares had started to feel like characters he knew. He thought of iron as the protagonist of the metals, the one everybody leaned on, hiding behind Fe like it had a secret identity. He texted one last challenge to the group. "Fe. Protons. Five seconds." Before he even put the phone down, the screen lit up with two answers, both reading 26.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: For a metal wire at constant temperature, a graph of voltage against current is a straight line through zero, and its slope is the resistance.
story:
Arthur waited until the science room emptied before he unpacked the shoebox, because the multimeter inside belonged to his uncle, who had lost his repair shop in the recession and now fixed toasters in the garage. "Borrow it as long as you need," his uncle had said, which Arthur understood to mean forever, or close to it.

The science fair was in three days, and Arthur's project was a mess. He had clipped the meter to a length of copper wire, pushed current through it, and written down five pairs of numbers: voltage and current, over and over. On their own the numbers were ambiguous. Divide one pair and he got a slightly different answer from the next pair, so which was the resistance of the wire, the number everyone was supposed to report? He had tried averaging, which felt like guessing with extra steps.

Shiloh leaned over his shoulder at the lab table. "Just pick the biggest one."

"That's not a method," Arthur said. "That's a shrug with math on it."

Mr. Desir drifted past on his rounds and tapped the graph paper lying blank beside the box. "Graphs nurture better thinking than tables do," he said, and moved on before Arthur could ask what that meant.

Arthur decided to try it anyway. He drew an x-axis for current and a y-axis for voltage, then plotted all five points. Something clicked in his chest. The points fell into a nearly perfect line, and when he held his ruler up and extended the line backward, it ran straight through the origin, through zero on both axes. Every reading, all at once, was telling him one thing instead of five confusing things. He grabbed his pencil and worked the slope, the rise over the run, using two points that were far apart so his measurement would be clean. When he divided, the number matched his best pair almost exactly.

Miguel came back from washing his hands, saw the graph, and frowned at it. "So which reading wins?"

"None of them," Arthur said. "Together they win. The slope is the resistance."

Miguel squinted at the line through zero, then at the shoebox meter, then back at the line. "So your uncle's toaster shop is basically why your project works."

"Basically," Arthur said, and drew a second wire's points on the same axes, watching them climb a steeper line than the first.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Under Robert's Rules, a tie vote means a motion fails, because it has not won more than half of the votes cast.
story:
Joshua set the folding table on Grandma's porch before anyone arrived, because the last meeting had fallen apart when three people talked at once and nobody could hear the vote. He had an agenda written in his grandfather's careful block letters: call to order, minutes, field trip vote, closing. When Kevin and Emerson climbed the porch steps, Joshua tapped the paper. "We follow this. One speaker at a time."

Grandpa's garage smelled like oil and cut lemons from the tree outside, and the boys dragged lawn chairs into the shade while Joshua read the agenda aloud. Kevin immediately pushed for the lake trip. "Canoes. All day. My uncle can drive." Emerson shook his head and raised his hand, which surprised Joshua, since Emerson never raised his hand. "The planetarium," Emerson said. "The new dome show is only on Saturdays, and Saturday is the one day my mom works, so she can't drive anywhere."

Both sides made sense, so Joshua called the vote. Kevin put up a hand. Emerson put up a hand. Joshua, who had planned to vote last so he wouldn't push anyone, looked down at his own hand and froze. "If I vote for the lake, it's two to one and we go to the lake."

"No," Emerson said, leaning forward. "You're the chair. If you vote, it's two to two." He said it flat, like a door closing. Joshua had read a chapter of Grandpa's old club handbook, the one with the cracked spine, and now he flipped through it fast, pages whispering. There it was, under motions and votes. He read the line twice under his breath.

"A tie vote means the motion fails," Joshua said. He emphasized the last word, and the porch went quiet except for a wasp ticking against the screen door. "It hasn't won more than half the votes cast, so it just doesn't pass. That's the rule." Kevin slumped. "So no lake?" "And no planetarium," Emerson said, which was an abrupt end to a whole afternoon of arguing, and both of them stared at Joshua like he had made it up.

Joshua thought about it, testing the idea against what he'd read. The rule wasn't the problem. The rule was just telling them something they already knew but hadn't said out loud. He picked up his pencil. "New motion. We table the trip vote until next meeting, and before then we ask the planetarium if they do weekday shows for groups." Kevin sat up. Emerson drummed his fingers on the chair arm, then nodded once. "Write it in the minutes," he said. Joshua wrote it, and the pencil scratched a small, steady line across the page.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
story:
On Thursday afternoon, Quinn sat at the upright piano in the music classroom and missed the same six notes for the eleventh time. The passage sat in the middle of her recital piece, a quick run that crossed her left hand over her right, and every time she reached it her fingers bunched up like dropped spaghetti. Ty leaned on the piano from the other side, watching. "You're slowing down right before it," he said. "Maybe stop being scared of it." Cassandra, who was waiting for her turn on the xylophone, was skeptical. "That's not it. She slows down because her hands don't know it yet. Watching harder won't fix that."

Ms. Whitehead came over and told Ty his bus would leave without him if he didn't commute to the gym for practice, so he left, but before he went he said, "Don't practice all night. Sleep on it." Quinn stayed another twenty minutes. She played the run slowly, then faster, then got it wrong, then got it wrong again, then packed up and went home with her practice sheet pressed flat in her bag.

That evening she did not touch the piano. She thought about Ty's advice and decided to test it, since her usual method, repeating the passage until her hands ached, had produced nothing all week. She ate dinner, read two chapters of a book about weather anomalies, and went to bed at nine. Lying in the dark, she felt the shape of the six notes in her fingers without moving them, then fell asleep.

On Friday morning the music classroom was open early, and Cassandra was already there tuning the xylophone. Quinn took the same bench, set the practice sheet on the stand, and played the passage straight through. Her left hand crossed over her right and landed on the exact keys, clean, twice, three times in a row. Cassandra put down her mallet and stared. "When did you practice that?"

"I didn't," Quinn said. "Not after Thursday. I slept on it, like Ty said. A night of sleep after practicing a sequence like this can make it better the next day without any extra practice." She said it plainly, the way she had read it in the science magazine at her dentist's office, because Cassandra was already frowning.

"That's an anomaly," Cassandra said.

"It happened, though. Watch." Quinn set her hands on the keys and played the six notes again, faster this time, and this time she did not slow down at all.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
story:
The living room was so packed that Addison had to sit on an overturned laundry basket, and the smell of her father's chili had begun to saturate every corner of the house. On the screen, two teams walked out onto the pitch for the final, and that was when the argument started.

"Brazil," said her uncle, pointing his spoon at the television. "Brazil won the first World Cup. Everyone knows that."

"Argentina," said Braylon, who had come over with a bowl of popcorn and a lot of confidence. "My grandfather told me. Argentina, all the way back."

Addison frowned. Something about both answers bothered her, though she couldn't have said why at first. She kept thinking while the announcer's voice filled the room, and then it clicked: nobody had actually named the country that hosted the very first tournament. Hosting and winning weren't necessarily the same thing, but if she could find out who hosted it, she'd be closer to the truth. She raised her hand like she was in Ms. Boateng's class and said, "Does anyone know where the first one was even played?"

"Europe somewhere," her uncle said vaguely.

The wifi was out because of the storm, so the plumbing of the internet, as her mother called the router in the hall closet, was useless. Addison went to the basement instead, where the family's old encyclopedias lived on sagging shelves. Carina followed her with a flashlight. "You really think it's down here?" Carina asked.

"It's a temporary blackout, not the end of information," Addison said, and pulled the volume with the right letter off the shelf. They knelt on the cold concrete floor and turned the thin pages until Carina sat back on her heels and read aloud: "First World Cup, 1930. Hosted and won by Uruguay, who beat Argentina four goals to two in the final."

They ran upstairs. "Uruguay," Addison announced, holding the book above her head like a trophy. "The first World Cup was in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina four to two."

Braylon stared at her. "My grandfather is going to be so upset."

"He can take it up with the encyclopedia," Addison said.

At halftime, her uncle slid the book toward himself and read the page twice, his lips moving. Then he closed it gently, stood up, and unclipped the spare key from his keyring. "Temporary custody," he said, laying the key in Addison's palm. "The trailer has the rest of the set. Go get the S through Z before your mother donates them."

Carina was already grabbing the flashlight.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like sawdust and lemon dish soap, because the downstairs bathroom was being renovated and everyone had to wash up at the sink by the back door. Evan spread his science kit across the counter: a stack of litmus paper, a chart of the pH scale, and five little jars he'd brought in his backpack.

"Ms. Krause said we have to test real things, not just stuff from the lab," Evan said. "So I'm testing everything in this house."

Lee pulled a bottle of vinegar from the pantry. Yazan found baking soda under the sink and grinned. "These two are going to fight each other. I've seen my mom do it."

Evan tore a strip of litmus paper in half and dipped one piece into a cup of vinegar mixed with water. The paper turned red. He checked the chart. "Three," he said. "Acid. Now the baking soda." He stirred a pinch of it into a fresh cup and dipped the other strip. It turned blue. He lined the two papers up on the counter like evidence.

"Try the soap," Lee said, nodding at the pink bar in the dish by the tap. "My grandpa swears by that stuff. Says his hands are a chronic mess from the machine shop and it's the only soap that cleans them."

Evan held the bar under the running water, worked up a puddle of suds in a cup, and dipped a fresh strip. He waited. The paper turned blue, a deeper blue than the baking soda had given him.

"That's weird," Evan said. "Soap should be neutral. It's just soap."

"Test it again," Yazan said.

"I tested it. Look." He laid the strip beside the others and measured it against the chart. "Nine. Maybe ten." He counted the boxes between the vinegar's three and the soap's nine, six whole squares on the scale, on the opposite side from the acid. "Most bar soaps are basic, around nine or ten," he said slowly, reading it off the chart's fine print. "This one's right there."

"So the stuff you wash with is on the base side of the scale," Lee said.

"Opposite from vinegar." Evan wrote it in his notebook, then looked up. "Grandpa!" he called toward the living room. "Your soap is a base!"

His grandfather appeared in the doorway with a cookie in one hand. "It's a what?"

"A base. Like the opposite of vinegar. Look." Evan held up the blue strip next to the red one. Grandpa leaned over the counter, squinting, and crumbs fell onto the pH chart.

"Huh," Grandpa said. "All these years." He went back to his chair, and Evan heard him tell someone on the phone, "The boy says my soap's a base."

Yazan was already eyeing the fish tank in the hall. "Can we test that next? There might be larva in the water from those plants."

Evan tore off three more strips and followed him.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him.
story:
Rose stood at the low stone wall of the war memorial, her notes flapping in the wind, and tried to say her presentation out loud for the fourth time. "The Treaty of Versailles," she began, "punished Germany after the First World War, and the Rhineland was supposed to stay demilitarized." That was as far as she got before her own voice faded. She could recite the facts, but she could not yet explain how a treaty signed in 1919 helped lead to a second war. It felt like tracing a river underground. She knew where it started and where it ended, but the part in between was hidden.

She tried again, walking slowly along the wall of carved names. "In March 1936," she said, "Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles." She paused by a name worn almost smooth. "And Britain and France did not use force to stop him." That part she could say perfectly. What she could not answer was Mr. Hernández's question from class, the one he had written on the board in his cramped handwriting: so what?

Behind her, Paul and Manraj were supposed to be copying names for their own assignment. Paul, though, had climbed onto the base of the memorial to rub a chalk impression of a name, even though the sign by the gate said clearly not to touch the stone. Mr. Hernández, who was helping another student across the lawn, didn't notice. Paul jumped down, grinning. "See? Nobody said anything."

"Because he didn't see you," Manraj said. "That's not the same as it being fine."

Rose watched Paul study the sign, then study Mr. Hernández's turned back, and she felt something click, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. A rule broken once, with no consequence, and now Paul was looking at the memorial's tall centrepiece, the one fenced off completely, and testing whether he could get away with more.

"Try it and Mr. Hernández will actually do something this time," Rose said. "You're not negotiating with a sign. You're negotiating with whether he acts."

"Feasible, though," Paul said, one hand on the fence. "I could get up there."

"That's not the point." Rose came closer, and the idea she had been chasing all morning finally lined itself up. What if 1936 worked the same way? Not the treaty itself, she thought, but what happened after it was broken. The treaty drew a line, and then the line got crossed, and the people who could have stopped it did not use force. She could distinguish between the rule and the response to the rule, and that was exactly the difference her presentation needed. The punishment in the treaty wasn't the whole story. What mattered was what the other countries did when it was broken.

She flipped her notes over and wrote on the blank back of the page, fast, while the sentences were still hot: the line was crossed in March 1936, and when crossing it cost nothing, the next crossing became thinkable. Paul was already halfway up the fence when Mr. Hernández's voice cracked across the lawn like a whip.

"Down. Now." Paul slid back to the grass, ears red, and Rose capped her pen. She walked to the gate with her notes against her chest and read the new paragraph once more. "So that's the so what," she said to Manraj, and pointed back at Paul, who was still apologizing. "Watch him. Now he'll never try the fence again. Now imagine nobody had said anything."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Lac des Pins smelled of pine and warm keyboards, and Maeva had claimed the seat by the window because the afternoon light made the screen easier to read. Her Python program was almost done. It asked for a number, tested whether anything divided it, and printed PRIME or NOT PRIME. She had been at it for three days, and today she wanted to finish before the swimming block so she could show Matthieu.

Rachel leaned over from the next computer, her own program still a blank file. "Type in a one," she said. "Test the weird cases first. That's what my sister does."

Maeva typed 1 and pressed Enter. The screen said PRIME. She frowned, because the little knot in her stomach said otherwise. She waved Matthieu over anyway, since he had promised to try her program, and he typed 7, then 9, then 100, and the answers all looked right. Then Mr. Jean-Louis, the activity leader, stopped behind them with his mug of coffee and peered at the screen through his transparent glasses, which fogged slightly at the edges.

"Try one," he said.

Matthieu typed it. PRIME. "See, it works," he said, but Mr. Jean-Louis only raised an eyebrow and waited, the way he did when he wanted campers to excavate the answer themselves instead of handing it to them. Maeva stared at the screen. She knew her loop checked divisors from 2 upward, so of course nothing divided 1, and the program called it prime. But something nagged at her. She grabbed the scrap paper by the keyboard and wrote out small numbers as products: 6 is 2 times 3, 12 is 2 times 2 times 3, 8 is 2 times 2 times 2. Every one had its own building blocks. Then she tried to write 1 that way and got nothing but a bare, lonely 1.

"Oh," she said. "One is not a prime number. Mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." She said it slowly, testing it as she went, and Mr. Jean-Louis nodded once and drifted off toward the canoe group. Maeva felt her cheeks go warm with a flash of embarrassment at her mistake, but Rachel was already grinning at her, and that made it easier.

"Your turn is coming," Maeva told her, adding the fix to her program, one line that turned 1 away at the door before the loop even began. She saved the file, spun her chair toward Rachel's blank screen, and dragged it closer. "Okay. First word of the day: print."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
The community centre piano room smelled of floor polish and old coffee, and the radiator by the window ticked like a slow metronome. Noemie spread her new sheet music on the stand, a short piece by a composer she had never heard of, printed with Italian words scattered between the staves. Her friend Aniya leaned over her shoulder, tapping one of them with a chipped fingernail.

"Andante," Aniya read. "That one's got to be fast, right? It sounds fast. Like running."

Noemie wasn't so sure. The word sat over a row of long, unhurried notes, half notes and whole notes, the kind you couldn't rush even if you tried. "Maybe it means something else," she said slowly. "There's a guy who plays here on Saturdays. He had a tote bag once with all these words printed on it."

Aniya rolled her eyes. "We're not going to interrogate a stranger about his tote bag."

They were saved from that particular controversy by Mr. Ong, who ran the Tuesday evening keyboard group and was stacking chairs in the corner. He wasn't a piano teacher exactly, more the person who kept the room booked and the radiator from flooding, but Noemie had seen him humming along when she practiced, so she raised her hand anyway.

"Mr. Ong, do you know what andante means? I think it might mean walking speed, but Aniya thinks fast." She had guessed it from the notes themselves, the way they strolled instead of sprinted, like someone crossing the community centre lobby without hurry.

Mr. Ong set down a chair. "Andante, a walking pace," he said. "Largo is very slow. Allegro is fast and lively." Then he went back to his chairs, offering nothing more, which was his way.

Noemie slid onto the bench. She played the opening, which was marked largo, and let each note sink into the room like a stone into still water. When andante arrived, she imagined her feet on the linoleum hallway outside, steady, unhurried, and the melody picked itself up and walked with her. Then the page turned and allegro flashed at the top, and her fingers had to leap, light and quick, like they'd been pollinated by something that made them suddenly busy.

Aniya had been right about one thing, sort of. "Okay," she admitted, from her seat on the radiator, "I would have played that walking part like a racehorse. The whole piece would have fallen apart by bar eight."

"It would have," Noemie agreed, "because you'd have been at allegro speed during andante." She played the passage again, this time shaping it even more, soft in the largo, fuller where the notes clustered lush and close together in the middle section, bright and skipping at the allegro. The room held the sound the way the window held the last of the evening light.

Mr. Ong stopped stacking chairs. He stood near the doorway with the last chair still in his hands, listening.

"You know," he said, "we could use a keyboard for the spring concert. Saturday mornings."

Noemie looked at the music on the stand, at all those Italian words she could now read like a map. "I'll be here," she said, and turned back to the first page, hands ready over the keys.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
Isabelle pressed her eye to the microscope at the museum's wet lab station and saw nothing but a pale gray blur. Behind her, Jannah was already sketching her slide, and the worksheet in Isabelle's pocket had three empty labels waiting: cell wall, membrane, nucleus. The class had forty minutes before the bus left, and Ms. Rahimi had made it clear that a finished worksheet was the price of the trip counting for science credit. A legitimate excuse, like a broken scope, might earn mercy, but nobody was going to believe a blur.

She twisted the coarse focus one way, then the other, slow as turning a safe dial. On the third try the blur sharpened into a lattice, rows of brick-shaped cells fitting edge to edge like a honeycomb flattened by a thumb. Isabelle blinked. The cells had been there the whole time, hidden inside an ordinary onion, waiting under a square of glass no bigger than a stamp.

"That's the cell wall," Jannah said, leaning over from the next stool. "The thick outer lines. The membrane's the skinny line hugging inside it." Isabelle copied the labels, then stopped at the dark dot floating in each cell. "And that's the nucleus," Charli said from across the bench. "That dark spot." Isabelle squinted at it. Somebody had to be the first person ever to notice that spot, she thought, back when nobody knew what a cell even was. She raised her hand. "Ms. Rahimi, do you know who first saw the nucleus?"

"Robert Brown," Ms. Rahimi said. "A Scottish botanist. He described the cell nucleus in 1831, while he was studying orchid cells." Isabelle wrote it in the margin of her worksheet. Charli leaned over to read it and frowned. "No way. People couldn't even see germs back then, so how did they figure out what caused infections? I thought all this stuff was modern." Isabelle tapped the margin with her pencil. "They didn't know about germs, that's the point. Brown saw the spot before anybody knew what it did. It took a whole lot longer, like a century, before doctors had an antibiotic to cure infections." Charli chewed her lip, looking from the margin to her own slide. "Huh. I guess you can find a thing long before you understand it." She crossed out something in her notes and started over.

Isabelle went back to her microscope, wanting to excavate every detail before the clock ran out, the faint membrane line, the nucleus like a small dark moon in each cell. But when she reached for the fine focus, her sleeve caught the stage and the slide skidded sideways. The image collapsed into blur again. Ms. Rahimi called five minutes from the doorway, and there was no time to re-center it properly. Isabelle got the wall back, just barely, and traced a shaky line where the membrane should be, but the nucleus had drifted to the edge of the field, half swallowed by shadow. She labeled it anyway, arrow pointing at the half-visible dot, and slid the worksheet into her folder as the lights over the benches clicked off.

On the bus, Jannah passed her a perfect drawing of all three labels, offering to let her copy it. Isabelle looked at it for a long moment, then handed it back. "Mine's a mess," she said, "but it's my mess. And I got the margin note." She turned to the window, where the museum was shrinking behind the trees. "Robert Brown, orchids, 1831," she said quietly, like a spell she didn't want to forget.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
At dinner, Sadie set her notebook next to her plate and pushed the green beans around with her fork. Tomorrow morning she had to hand in her survey project for Mr. Flores, and right now it was wrong.

"Smells good," she said, mostly to herself. Her mother had made the spicy noodle casserole from the box labeled with the school logo, the same snack the cafeteria was considering adding next month. Sadie had surveyed three people: Sami, Kate, and her older brother. All three loved it. She had written her conclusion in bold letters: "Everyone loves this snack."

Her dad spooned a second helping onto his plate. "Two people at my office tried it today," he said. "One spit it into a napkin."

Sadie put down her fork. Three out of three loved it, but one out of two hated it. The numbers were pointing in opposite directions. She flipped to her results page and stared at her three tally marks. Then she remembered Kate saying something at lunch about Mr. Flores's class survey, the big one taken during first period.

"Can I use the phone?" she asked, already reaching for it. She texted Sami: "Did you do Flores's class survey about the noodle thing?" The answer came back a minute later with a photo of the results sheet. Two hundred students had answered. One hundred and eighteen said "okay," forty-one said "love it," and the rest said "no."

Sadie ran the numbers twice. In two hundred people, "love it" was the smallest group. Her survey of three had made it look like everyone. She picked up her pencil, crossed out her bold conclusion, and started writing new lines: a claim about what people think needs tested evidence, and a story about three friends tasting something is not that. Three people can all happen to love it, she wrote, but in two hundred the differences even out.

She paused over the word "evidence," then circled it. Her claim would be: "Most students think this snack is just okay." The big survey was her evidence, and she could quantify exactly how it backed her up. Her brother's glowing review now looked ambiguous, one voice that could mean anything.

"Bed by ten," her mom said, clearing plates. "Deadline's at eight-thirty, not midnight."

"I know." Sadie copied the results onto a fresh page. Her dad, a veteran of twenty years of Friday-night office snack orders, leaned over her shoulder.

"Two hundred answers beat three," he said.

"That's the whole point," Sadie said, and stapled the pages together.
